question: What is the GIL and when does it actually limit you?
expected_concepts: only one thread executes bytecode at a time
CPU-bound work does not scale across threads
I/O-bound work and C extensions can release it
answer: The GIL is a mutex in CPython that lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time. So threads do not help CPU-bound work - you want multiprocessing or a C extension for that. It does get released during blocking I/O and inside some C extensions like numpy, which is why threaded I/O still scales fine.
note: All three concepts, with the correct nuance about when it is released.

question: Why would you return a generator instead of a list?
expected_concepts: lazy evaluation, one item at a time
constant memory instead of holding everything
can represent infinite or very large sequences
answer: A generator yields items one at a time instead of building the whole list in memory, so memory stays flat no matter how many items there are. That matters when you are streaming a huge file - you never hold more than one row.
note: Laziness and memory are solid; never reaches infinite sequences.

question: What is the difference between `is` and `==`?
expected_concepts: `is` compares identity
`==` compares value via __eq__
small int and string interning can mislead
answer: `is` checks whether two names point to the same object, `==` checks whether the values are equal. You use `is` for None.
note: Identity and value correct; no mention of interning surprises.

question: How does a decorator work?
expected_concepts: a callable that takes a function and returns a function
applied with @ at definition time
functools.wraps preserves metadata
answer: A decorator wraps a function to add behaviour around it. You put @something above the def.
note: States the shape but not the mechanism; no return-a-callable, no wraps.

question: Explain `async`/`await` and when it helps.
expected_concepts: cooperative concurrency on a single thread
await yields control at I/O boundaries
no benefit for CPU-bound work
answer: Async makes your code run faster because it uses multiple cores to do things in parallel. You add async to a function and it automatically becomes multithreaded.
note: Confidently wrong: conflates async with parallelism and multithreading.

question: What problem do context managers solve?
expected_concepts: deterministic acquire/release
cleanup runs even when an exception is raised
__enter__/__exit__ or contextlib
answer: They guarantee cleanup. `with open(...)` closes the file whether the block finishes normally or raises, because __exit__ runs either way. You can write your own with __enter__/__exit__ or @contextmanager.
note: Correct and complete on the mechanism; light on why deterministic timing matters.

question: Why is a mutable default argument a bug?
expected_concepts: the default is evaluated once at def time
the same object is shared across calls
use None as the sentinel instead
answer: Because the list gets reused between calls, so things you append in one call show up in the next one. The fix is to default to None and build the list inside.
note: Knows the symptom and the fix, but not that evaluation happens once at def time.

question: Shallow copy versus deep copy?
expected_concepts: shallow copies the outer container only
nested objects stay shared
deepcopy recurses and handles cycles
answer: Copying objects in Python is an important topic. There are different ways to copy and you should pick the right one depending on your use case, since it affects performance and correctness.
note: Topically relevant, says nothing specific - the case the divergence check should catch.

question: How does dependency injection work in FastAPI?
expected_concepts: Depends() declares what a handler needs
FastAPI resolves the tree before the handler runs
results are cached per request
answer: You declare a parameter as Depends(something) and FastAPI calls that function first and passes you the result. It resolves the whole tree of dependencies, and within one request each dependency runs once - so two things that both depend on get_db share the same session.
note: All three, including the per-request caching that most answers miss.

question: What does a dependency with `yield` give you?
expected_concepts: setup before the handler, teardown after
teardown runs even on an exception
the common pattern for a DB session or transaction
answer: Everything before the yield runs before your handler, everything after runs once it returns. That is how get_db opens a session and commits or rolls back afterwards - the teardown still runs if the handler raised.
note: Setup/teardown and the DB case are right; does not generalise beyond it.

question: What is `response_model` for?
expected_concepts: validates the outgoing payload
filters fields not declared on the model
drives the OpenAPI schema
answer: It tells FastAPI what shape to return and it shows up in the docs at /docs so clients know what to expect.
note: Documentation role is right; misses that it actively filters undeclared fields.

question: When would you use BackgroundTasks instead of Celery?
expected_concepts: BackgroundTasks runs in the same process after the response
work is lost if the process dies
Celery survives restarts and scales to other machines
answer: BackgroundTasks is for small things you want to do after responding, like sending an email. Celery is for heavier work. BackgroundTasks is simpler because there is no broker to run.
note: Right instinct and the simplicity trade-off, but never says the work is not durable.

question: How does Pydantic validation fit into a request?
expected_concepts: body is parsed and validated before the handler
a failure returns 422 with field errors
the handler only ever sees valid data
answer: Pydantic checks the types of the incoming data and raises an error if something is wrong.
note: True but thin: no 422, no handler-never-sees-bad-input guarantee.

question: Should a path operation be `async def` or `def`?
expected_concepts: async def runs on the event loop
def runs in a threadpool so it cannot block the loop
blocking I/O inside async def stalls every other request
answer: Use async def when you are awaiting async libraries. If you use plain def, FastAPI runs it in a thread pool so a blocking call does not freeze the server. The trap is doing blocking work inside an async def - that blocks the whole event loop and every other request behind it.
note: Correct on all three; slightly muddled on which to default to.

question: What is middleware used for?
expected_concepts: wraps every request and response
cross-cutting concerns like CORS or logging
runs outside the route's dependency tree
answer: Middleware is where you put your business logic so it can be shared between endpoints. It is basically the same as a dependency but you register it once.
note: Wrong: middleware is not where business logic goes, and it is not equivalent to a dependency.

question: Why set an explicit `status_code` on a route?
expected_concepts: 201 for created, 202 for accepted, 204 for no content
the default 200 is often a lie
clients and the OpenAPI schema depend on it
answer: So the client gets the right code back instead of always 200.
note: Gestures at the idea without naming a single code or consequence.

question: How does an index change query performance, and what does it cost?
expected_concepts: turns a sequential scan into a lookup
writes get slower, storage grows
only helps if the query can use it (leading column, no function on the column)
answer: An index lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of scanning the table, so reads get much faster. The cost is that every insert and update has to maintain the index too, and it takes disk space. It also only helps if the query actually matches it - wrapping the column in a function, or filtering on the second column of a composite index, means it gets ignored.
note: Reads, write cost, and the usability condition that most answers skip.

question: What is the N+1 query problem?
expected_concepts: one query for the list, one per row after that
latency scales with row count
fixed by a join or an eager load
answer: You fetch a list with one query and then loop over it firing another query per item, so 100 rows means 101 round trips. You fix it by joining or eager-loading the relation up front.
note: Mechanism and fix both correct; does not name latency as the cost.

question: What does a transaction isolation level control?
expected_concepts: what concurrent transactions can see of each other
anomalies: dirty/non-repeatable/phantom reads
stricter levels cost concurrency
answer: It controls how isolated transactions are from each other. Read committed is the Postgres default and stops you reading uncommitted data.
note: Correct default and one anomaly; no trade-off, no other anomalies.

question: Explain the difference between INNER and LEFT JOIN.
expected_concepts: INNER keeps only matching rows
LEFT keeps all left rows, NULLs on the right
a WHERE on the right column silently turns LEFT into INNER
answer: INNER JOIN only returns rows that match in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns everything from the left table and fills in NULL where there is no match.
note: Both joins correct; misses the WHERE-clause trap, which is the interesting part.

question: When would you use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE?
expected_concepts: locks the selected rows for the transaction
prevents concurrent modification between read and write
risks deadlock if lock order is inconsistent
answer: It locks the rows you select so nobody else can change them while you are working.
note: First concept only; no read-modify-write framing, no deadlock risk.

question: Why normalise a schema, and when would you not?
expected_concepts: removes duplication so updates touch one place
reduces anomalies
denormalise deliberately for read performance
answer: Normalisation means splitting data into separate tables so you do not repeat yourself. It is generally considered good practice in database design.
note: Definition without consequence; never reaches anomalies or the denormalisation trade-off.

question: What do you look for in an EXPLAIN plan?
expected_concepts: scan type: sequential versus index
row estimates versus actual rows
where the time is actually spent
answer: I check whether it is doing a sequential scan where I expected an index, and I compare the estimated rows to the actual rows - if the planner estimate is way off, the statistics are stale and it is picking a bad plan. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows where the time really goes.
note: Strong and practical; does not mention cost units or buffers.

question: Why use a connection pool?
expected_concepts: opening a connection is expensive
bounds concurrent load on the database
connections are reused across requests
answer: A connection pool makes the database faster by caching query results so repeated queries do not have to hit the disk again.
note: Wrong: describes a query cache, not a connection pool.

question: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
expected_concepts: single-threaded with a task queue
callbacks run when the stack is empty
microtasks (promises) drain before macrotasks
answer: JS runs on one thread with a call stack. Async work is handed to the browser or Node, and when it finishes the callback goes on a queue. The loop only picks something off the queue once the stack is empty. Promise callbacks go on the microtask queue, which drains completely before the next timer or I/O callback runs - that is why an await resolves before a setTimeout(0).
note: All three, with the microtask/macrotask ordering made concrete.

question: What is a closure and why is it useful?
expected_concepts: a function keeps access to its defining scope
the captured variables outlive the call
used for private state and factories
answer: A closure is when an inner function remembers the variables from the scope it was created in, even after the outer function has returned. It is how you get private state - a counter that only the returned function can touch.
note: Mechanism and privacy both right; does not mention factories or capture-by-reference.

question: Why did promises replace callbacks?
expected_concepts: flat chaining instead of nesting
errors propagate through .catch
composable: Promise.all and friends
answer: Promises let you chain .then instead of nesting callbacks inside callbacks, which gets unreadable fast. You also get .catch for errors.
note: Nesting and errors covered; nothing about composition.

question: `var`, `let`, `const` - what changes?
expected_concepts: var is function-scoped and hoisted
let/const are block-scoped with a temporal dead zone
const binds the name, not the value
answer: var is function scoped, let and const are block scoped. const means you cannot reassign it, though you can still mutate an object it points to.
note: Scope and the const nuance are right; no hoisting, no TDZ.

question: How does prototypal inheritance work?
expected_concepts: objects delegate to a prototype object
lookup walks the prototype chain
class syntax is sugar over the same mechanism
answer: Objects can inherit from other objects through the prototype. JavaScript uses this instead of classical inheritance.
note: Names the mechanism without explaining lookup or the class-syntax relationship.

question: `==` versus `===`?
expected_concepts: === compares without coercion
== applies type coercion rules
coercion produces surprising results, so prefer ===
answer: === is strict equality and == is loose. You should basically always use ===.
note: Correct advice, no mechanism - does not say what loose actually does.

question: Debounce versus throttle?
expected_concepts: debounce waits for a quiet period then fires once
throttle fires at most once per interval
debounce for search input, throttle for scroll or resize
answer: Debounce waits until the user stops doing the thing and then runs once - good for a search box so you do not fire a request per keystroke. Throttle runs at a fixed maximum rate no matter how often the event fires, which is what you want for scroll handlers.
note: Both definitions and both use cases; does not mention leading/trailing edge options.

question: How is `this` determined?
expected_concepts: depends on the call site, not the definition
arrow functions capture lexically
call/apply/bind set it explicitly
answer: `this` always refers to the object the function belongs to, so inside a class method it is the instance. Arrow functions work the same way as normal functions here.
note: Wrong on both counts: call-site rules and arrow lexical capture are the whole point.

question: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be idempotent, and why does it matter?
expected_concepts: the same request repeated has the same effect as once
GET/PUT/DELETE are idempotent, POST is not
lets clients and proxies retry safely
answer: Idempotent means sending the request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, because two POSTs usually create two resources. It matters because a client that times out can safely retry an idempotent request without worrying about duplicating anything - which is also why non-idempotent endpoints need an idempotency key.
note: All three plus the practical consequence for retries.

question: Walk through the HTTP status code families.
expected_concepts: 2xx success, 3xx redirect
4xx client error, 5xx server error
the class tells a client whether retrying can help
answer: 2xx means it worked, 3xx is a redirect, 4xx means the client did something wrong like a bad request or missing auth, and 5xx means the server broke.
note: All families correct; does not draw out the retry implication.

question: PUT versus PATCH?
expected_concepts: PUT replaces the whole resource
PATCH applies a partial update
PUT is idempotent; PATCH depends on the patch
answer: PUT replaces the entire resource with what you send, PATCH only updates the fields you include.
note: Core distinction right; nothing on idempotency.

question: What problem does CORS solve?
expected_concepts: browsers block cross-origin reads by default
the server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-* headers
preflight OPTIONS for non-simple requests
answer: CORS is what lets a frontend on one domain call an API on another. The server has to send headers allowing the origin, otherwise the browser blocks it.
note: Policy and server opt-in correct; no preflight, no browser-enforced-only.

question: How do HTTP caching headers work?
expected_concepts: Cache-Control sets freshness
ETag/If-None-Match enables revalidation
304 avoids re-sending the body
answer: You set Cache-Control to tell the browser how long it can cache a response.
note: One header, no validation story at all.

question: Cookies or bearer tokens for auth - what is the trade-off?
expected_concepts: cookies are sent automatically, so they need CSRF protection
bearer tokens are explicit but readable by JS, so XSS steals them
httpOnly cookies are not readable by JS
answer: Cookies get attached automatically by the browser, which is convenient but opens you to CSRF since any site can trigger the request. Bearer tokens have to be attached by your own code, so no CSRF, but if they are in localStorage then any XSS can read them. httpOnly cookies fix the XSS side but bring CSRF back.
note: All three trade-offs; does not mention SameSite as the modern CSRF mitigation.

question: What did HTTP/2 multiplexing change?
expected_concepts: many streams over one TCP connection
removes head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer
domain sharding and concatenation became counterproductive
answer: HTTP/2 can send multiple requests at the same time over one connection instead of opening several.
note: The headline only; no head-of-line blocking, no consequence for old workarounds.

question: What does it mean that REST is stateless?
expected_concepts: each request carries everything needed to process it
the server keeps no per-client session context
enables any instance to serve any request
answer: It means the server does not store any data. Everything has to be sent by the client each time, so REST APIs cannot use a database.
note: Wrong: confuses per-client session state with persistent storage.

question: Why put slow work on a queue instead of doing it in the request?
expected_concepts: the response returns immediately
work survives a dropped connection
workers scale and retry independently
answer: If the work takes 30 seconds you cannot hold the HTTP request open for it - the client times out and you lose the work if the connection drops. Putting a job on a queue lets you return 202 straight away, and the worker picks it up separately. You can then scale workers independently of the API and retry a failed job without the user being involved.
note: All three, with the 202 pattern made explicit.

question: Your queue guarantees at-least-once delivery. What does that force you to do?
expected_concepts: a message can be delivered more than once
handlers must be idempotent
dedupe by key or guard with a uniqueness constraint
answer: At-least-once means you might get the same message twice, so the handler has to be idempotent - running it a second time should not double-charge anyone. Usually you guard it with a unique key on the work you have already done.
note: All three in substance; does not distinguish from exactly-once or at-most-once.

question: How would you decide what to cache?
expected_concepts: read-heavy and expensive to compute
tolerable staleness
invalidation strategy decided up front
answer: Cache the things that get read a lot and do not change often, like a config lookup or a popular product page. You have to think about how stale it is allowed to get.
note: Read-heavy and staleness covered; invalidation - the hard part - is absent.

question: Horizontal versus vertical scaling?
expected_concepts: vertical = bigger machine, horizontal = more machines
vertical has a ceiling and a single point of failure
horizontal requires statelessness or shared state
answer: Vertical scaling is making the server bigger - more CPU and RAM. Horizontal is adding more servers behind a load balancer. Horizontal is usually preferred for large systems.
note: Definitions right; no ceiling/SPOF, no statelessness requirement.

question: What does a circuit breaker do?
expected_concepts: stops calling a dependency that is failing
fails fast instead of queueing behind a timeout
half-opens after a cooldown to probe recovery
answer: It stops sending requests to a service that is down so you do not make things worse.
note: First concept only; no fail-fast reasoning, no half-open probe.

question: How would you rate limit an API?
expected_concepts: a counter per client per window
token bucket allows bursts, fixed window does not
return 429 with Retry-After
answer: You would count requests per user and block them if they go over the limit. Redis is a common place to keep the counter.
note: Counting is right; no algorithm choice, no 429 contract.

question: When do read replicas help, and what do they cost?
expected_concepts: spread read load off the primary
replication lag means reads can be stale
writes still bottleneck on the primary
answer: Replicas take read traffic off the primary, which helps when you are read-heavy. The catch is replication lag - you can write something and then read a replica that has not caught up yet, so a user sees their own change missing. Writes all still go to the primary, so they do not help write throughput at all.
note: All three, clearly; does not name read-your-writes as the pattern.

question: Explain the CAP theorem.
expected_concepts: consistency, availability, partition tolerance
a partition forces a choice between C and A
partition tolerance is not optional in a distributed system
answer: CAP says you can pick any two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance. Most databases choose consistency and availability and drop partition tolerance.
note: The classic misreading: you cannot drop partition tolerance in a distributed system.
